newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels permit costly Hutu refugee airlift.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels permit costly Hutu refugee airlift.

text.p: The leader of Zaire's advancing rebels gave his permission on Saturday for a vastly expensive international airlift to repatriate up to 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees.

The agreement was announced in the rebel-held city of Kisangani by European Union (EU) special envoy Aldo Aiello and Emmanuel Kamenze, a senior official in Laurent Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL).

"I've got a message just a few minutes ago from Mr Kabila that the airport will be open and will be made available for the repatriation of refugees," Aiello told reporters in Kisangani, which fell to the rebels on March 15.

The rebels had earlier insisted the refugees, camped along a rail track south of Kisangani and reported dying at the rate of at least 120 a day, had to be repatriated by roads that are virtually impassable.

But the last two days of intense international pressure on the rebels, from the U.N. Security Council, the EU and U.N. agencies, apparently forced a change of mind on the same day the rebels sat down in South Africa for their first negotiations with President Mobutu Sese Seko's crippled regime.
The details of the refugee airlift were sketchy.
The head of the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR in rapidly expanding rebel-held Zaire, Filippo Grandi, said the operation could start in a few days and last two or three months.
"They will be flown by aircraft chartered by relief agencies," he said.
Grandi adjusted his earlier estimate it would cost $50 million to fly the 100,000 Hutus home, or about $500 each for the 90-minute flight.
"It is not going to cost $50 million. I was wrong, it may cost half that but we don't know precisely," he told reporters.
The Hutus, many emaciated and sick from malaria, dysentery and hunger, left their camps in eastern Zaire, close to Rwanda's border, six months ago.

They fled at the start of Kabila's rebellion last October and trekked up to 600 km (375 miles) across volcanic rock, bush and finally through deep tropical forest where they ate plants, bark and insects. Since late last month they have been strung out along a rail track that cuts through the jungle from Kisangani to Ubundu.
Now they say they want to go back to Rwanda which they fled in July 1994 with more than two million other Hutus, who have since gone home, after the victory of Tutsi rebels.

Many have reason to fear the return because they could be blamed for the 1994 genocide of minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus. More than 90,000 Hutus are in detention in Rwanda accused of genocide and a handful have already been sentenced to death.
Kabila's envoy, Kamenze, said at first the airlift would be for the sick but then said all refugees could be transported.

Rwanda's government must approve before the refugees can be flown directly to Kigali, the capital. The other option, Grandi and Kamenze said, was to fly them to rebel headquarters at Goma and truck them the last few kms (miles) into Rwanda.

Aiello said Kabila had recognised his interest was to rid himself quickly of the "liability" of the refugees. The issue was turning into the rebels' first major public relations setback and the concession has cost them little, analysts said.
The priority for Kabila is to continue his almost unopposed march through Zaire while resisting calls for a ceasefire.
